title: Clustering with K-Means
summary: Clustering is the most common unsupervised learning task, where you group similar data points together without any labels, and K-Means is the classic algorithm for it. K-Means works by choosing k cluster centers, assigning each point to its nearest c
content:
# Clustering with K-Means ##### The segmentation that found "people who own phones" A retail team in Ahmedabad ran K-Means on their customer database to find marketing segments. They fed in every column they had: total spend, order count, age, pincode, days since signup, and a customer ID. The algorithm produced five neat clusters. Then someone profiled them. Cluster 1: customer IDs 1–4,000. Cluster 2: IDs 4,001–8,000. And so on. The customer ID was a large-magnitude number that dominated every distance calculation, so K-Means had faithfully clustered people by *when they signed up in the database*. They removed the ID, scaled the remaining features, and reran. This time they got genuinely useful segments — high-frequency small-basket shoppers, occasional bulk buyers, dormant accounts, and a small premium group. Two lessons in one incident: **scaling is not optional**, and **K-Means will always give you clusters, whether or not they mean anything.** The algorithm cannot tell you your segmentation is nonsense. Only profiling can. ##### Unsupervised learning: no labels, no answer key Supervised learning has a target column and a clear notion of correctness. Unsupervised learning has neither. You are looking for structure that already exists in the data. | | Supervised | Unsupervised | |---|---|---| | Input | Features + labels | Features only | | Goal | Predict the label | Discover structure | | Evaluation | Compare to known answers | No ground truth — judgement required | | Risk | Overfitting | Finding patterns that are not real | That last row is the important one. A classifier that performs poorly announces itself with a bad test score. A clustering that is meaningless looks exactly like a clustering that is insightful. The burden of validation falls on you. The main unsupervised tasks: **clustering** (group similar items), **dimensionality reduction** (compress features), **anomaly detection** (find the unusual), and **association rules** (items bought together). ##### How K-Means works K-Means partitions data into k groups by minimising within-cluster variance. The algorithm — Lloyd's algorithm — is four steps: ``` 1. Choose k initial centroids 2. ASSIGN: each point joins its nearest centroid's cluster 3. UPDATE: each centroid moves to the mean of its assigned points 4. Repeat 2-3 until assignments stop changing ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Pick k initial centroids] --> B[Assign each point to
the nearest centroid] B --> C[Move each centroid to the
mean of its points] C --> D{Did any assignment change?} D -->|Yes| B D -->|No| E[Converged] E --> F[Repeat from different starts
keep the lowest inertia] ``` The objective it minimises is **inertia** — the sum of squared distances from each point to its assigned centroid: ``` inertia = Σ ||xᵢ − μ_{c(i)}||² ``` A from-scratch version makes it concrete: ```python import numpy as np def kmeans(X, k, max_iter=100, seed=42): rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) centroids = X[rng.choice(len(X), k, replace=False)] for _ in range(max_iter): # ASSIGN: distance from every point to every centroid d = np.linalg.norm(X[:, None, :] - centroids[None, :, :], axis=2) labels = d.argmin(axis=1) # UPDATE new = np.array([X[labels == j].mean(axis=0) if (labels == j).any() else centroids[j] for j in range(k)]) if np.allclose(new, centroids): break centroids = new inertia = ((X - centroids[labels]) ** 2).sum() return labels, centroids, inertia ``` Two properties follow from that loop. It always converges, but only to a **local** optimum — different starting centroids give different results. And it assumes clusters are roughly spherical and similarly sized, because it assigns by Euclidean distance to a mean. scikit-learn handles the local-optimum problem with `n_init`, which runs the whole algorithm several times from different starts and keeps the best: ```python from sklearn.cluster import KMeans km = KMeans(n_clusters=4, init="k-means++", n_init=10, random_state=42) labels = km.fit_predict(X_scaled) print(km.inertia_, km.n_iter_) ``` `init="k-means++"` is the default and worth knowing: instead of random starting points, it spreads the initial centroids apart probabilistically, which converges faster and lands in better optima. ##### Scaling is mandatory This is the Ahmedabad failure, and it deserves its own section because it is the single most common K-Means mistake. K-Means uses Euclidean distance. Distance sums contributions from every feature. A feature ranging over hundreds of thousands contributes hundreds of thousands; a feature ranging 1–10 contributes almost nothing. ```python import pandas as pd from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler df = pd.DataFrame({ "total_spend_inr": [45000, 120000, 8000, 220000, 15000], "order_count": [12, 8, 3, 15, 4], "days_since_last": [5, 45, 120, 2, 90], }) # Without scaling — spend dominates completely km_raw = KMeans(4, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(df) # With scaling — every feature contributes equally X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df) km_scaled = KMeans(4, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(X_scaled) print("raw :", km_raw.labels_) print("scaled:", km_scaled.labels_) ``` Run those two and compare. On real data the assignments usually differ substantially, and only the scaled version reflects all three behaviours rather than just spend. Which scaler: `StandardScaler` is the default. Use `RobustScaler` when outliers are present, since a single extreme customer will otherwise pull a centroid toward itself and create a cluster of one. Also relevant: **drop identifiers before clustering.** Customer IDs, row numbers and timestamps-as-integers carry no behavioural meaning but plenty of numeric magnitude. ##### Choosing k K-Means requires you to specify k in advance, and there is no objectively correct answer. Two standard methods, used together. **The elbow method** plots inertia against k. Inertia always decreases as k grows (with k = n, every point is its own cluster and inertia is zero), so you look for the point where the rate of improvement drops — the "elbow". ```python import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score ks = range(2, 12) inertias, silhouettes = [], [] for k in ks: km = KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(X_scaled) inertias.append(km.inertia_) silhouettes.append(silhouette_score(X_scaled, km.labels_)) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5)) axes[0].plot(ks, inertias, "o-") axes[0].set_xlabel("k"); axes[0].set_ylabel("inertia") axes[0].set_title("Elbow method — look for the bend") axes[1].plot(ks, silhouettes, "s-", color="#38a169") axes[1].set_xlabel("k"); axes[1].set_ylabel("silhouette score") axes[1].set_title("Silhouette — higher is better") best_k = list(ks)[int(np.argmax(silhouettes))] axes[1].axvline(best_k, color="red", ls="--", label=f"best k = {best_k}") axes[1].legend() fig.tight_layout() ``` The elbow is often ambiguous — many real curves bend smoothly with no obvious corner. That is why you pair it with a metric that has a clear optimum. **Silhouette score** measures, for each point, how much closer it is to its own cluster than to the nearest other cluster: ``` s = (b − a) / max(a, b) a = mean distance to points in its own cluster b = mean distance to points in the nearest other cluster ``` It ranges from −1 to +1: above 0.5 is reasonable structure, around 0.25 is weak, and negative means points are assigned to the wrong cluster. Unlike inertia, it has a genuine maximum, so `argmax` is meaningful. A silhouette plot shows the distribution within each cluster, which reveals more than the average: ```python from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_samples km = KMeans(best_k, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(X_scaled) sil = silhouette_samples(X_scaled, km.labels_) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6)) y_lower = 10 for i in range(best_k): vals = np.sort(sil[km.labels_ == i]) ax.fill_betweenx(np.arange(y_lower, y_lower + len(vals)), 0, vals, alpha=0.7) ax.text(-0.05, y_lower + len(vals) / 2, str(i)) y_lower += len(vals) + 10 ax.axvline(sil.mean(), color="red", ls="--", label=f"mean {sil.mean():.3f}") ax.set_xlabel("silhouette coefficient"); ax.legend() ``` A cluster whose bar is mostly below the mean line is poorly separated and probably should not exist as its own segment. Other options: `davies_bouldin_score` (lower is better) and `calinski_harabasz_score` (higher is better) provide corroboration. And crucially — **business constraints often decide k.** If marketing can run four campaigns, k = 4, regardless of what the silhouette says. ##### Profiling and interpreting clusters This is the step that separates a segmentation from a set of arbitrary group numbers, and it is where the Ahmedabad team caught their bug. ```python df["cluster"] = km.labels_ profile = df.groupby("cluster").agg( n=("total_spend_inr", "size"), avg_spend=("total_spend_inr", "mean"), avg_orders=("order_count", "mean"), avg_recency=("days_since_last", "mean"), ).round(1) profile["pct_of_base"] = (profile["n"] / len(df) * 100).round(1) print(profile) # How does each cluster differ from the overall average? overall = df[num_cols].mean() deviation = df.groupby("cluster")[num_cols].mean().sub(overall).div(overall).mul(100) print(deviation.round(1)) # percentage above/below the population average ``` That deviation table is the most useful output — it tells you what makes each cluster *distinctive* rather than just what its averages are. Visualise with a heatmap of standardised means: ```python import seaborn as sns centroid_df = pd.DataFrame( StandardScaler().fit(df[num_cols]).transform(km.cluster_centers_ @ np.eye(len(num_cols))), columns=num_cols) sns.heatmap(df.groupby("cluster")[num_cols].mean().apply( lambda c: (c - c.mean()) / c.std()), annot=True, cmap="coolwarm", center=0) ``` Then **name the clusters**. "Cluster 2" is not a deliverable; "Frequent small-basket regulars" is. A good naming pass produces something like: | Cluster | Name | Size | Profile | Action | |---|---|---|---|---| | 0 | Dormant | 34% | Low spend, 120+ days inactive | Win-back campaign | | 1 | Regulars | 41% | Moderate spend, frequent, recent | Loyalty programme | | 2 | Big-basket occasional | 19% | High spend, few orders | Bulk offers | | 3 | Premium | 6% | Very high spend, very frequent | Dedicated service | **Validate the segmentation before acting on it.** Three checks: are the clusters stable across different random seeds; do they differ on a variable you did *not* cluster on (a strong sign the structure is real); and does a domain expert recognise them? If your "segments" mean nothing to the person who runs the business, they are probably artefacts. ##### When K-Means is the wrong tool K-Means assumes spherical, similarly-sized, similarly-dense clusters. Real data often violates all three. | Problem | Symptom | Alternative | |---|---|---| | Elongated or curved clusters | K-Means slices them arbitrarily | `DBSCAN`, spectral clustering | | Very different cluster sizes | Large cluster gets split | `GaussianMixture` | | Outliers | They pull centroids or form singleton clusters | `DBSCAN` (labels them noise) | | Unknown k | You must guess | `DBSCAN`, hierarchical | | Non-numeric features | Distance is undefined | `k-modes`, Gower distance | | Very high dimensions | Distances become meaningless | PCA first, then cluster | ```python from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN, AgglomerativeClustering from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture DBSCAN(eps=0.5, min_samples=5).fit_predict(X_scaled) # -1 marks noise points AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=4).fit_predict(X_scaled) GaussianMixture(n_components=4, random_state=42).fit_predict(X_scaled) ``` DBSCAN is worth knowing as the main alternative: it finds arbitrarily-shaped clusters, determines the number itself, and explicitly labels outliers as noise rather than forcing them into a group. ##### Common mistakes - Clustering without scaling — the single most common error. - Leaving IDs, row numbers or timestamps in the feature set. - Reading the elbow plot alone when it has no clear bend. - Never computing a silhouette score to sanity-check the structure. - `n_init=1`, so the result depends on one arbitrary initialisation. - Not setting `random_state`, so the segmentation changes every run. - Assuming clusters are meaningful without profiling them. - Leaving clusters labelled 0–4 instead of naming and describing them. - Applying K-Means to elongated or wildly unequal clusters. - Clustering on 200 features without reducing dimensions first. ##### Hands-on Take a dataset with several numeric behavioural features. Scale them, run K-Means across k = 2 to 12, and produce both the elbow and silhouette plots side by side. Pick a k, then profile every cluster: size, mean of each feature, and percentage deviation from the population average. Deliberately run the same clustering *without* scaling and compare the assignments — reproducing the Ahmedabad failure on your own data is the fastest way to make the lesson stick. For the mini-project, build a customer segmentation end to end. Choose k using both methods plus a stated business constraint, visualise the clusters in two dimensions (PCA projection works well for this, which is tomorrow's topic), write a descriptive profile and a business recommendation for each segment, and give each a memorable name. Add a validation section: check stability across three random seeds, and test whether the clusters differ significantly on a variable you excluded from the clustering. That external check is what turns a plausible segmentation into a defensible one. For the assignment, cluster a dataset with two different k values — say 3 and 6 — and write a comparison of how the interpretation changes. Argue for which is more useful, and be specific about the trade-off: fewer clusters are easier to act on but blur real differences, while more clusters are precise but may split a group that behaves identically for business purposes. ##### Key takeaways - K-Means minimises within-cluster variance by alternating assignment and centroid updates — and always converges to a local optimum. - Scaling is mandatory, and identifiers must be removed, or distance is dominated by whichever column has the biggest numbers. - Use the elbow *and* silhouette together; inertia always falls with k, so it has no natural optimum. - The algorithm always returns clusters — profiling, naming and external validation are what determine whether they mean anything. - K-Means assumes spherical, similar-sized clusters; reach for DBSCAN or Gaussian mixtures when that fails.
practical_task_reference: Scale a dataset's features, run K-Means for several values of k, use the elbow method and silhouette score to pick k, then profile each resulting cluster.
mini_project_reference: Build a customer (or similar) segmentation project that clusters a dataset, chooses k with proper methods, visualizes the clusters, and writes a descriptive profile and business interpretation for each segment.
assignment_reference: Cluster a dataset with two different k values and write a comparison of how the interpretation changes, arguing for which k is more useful.
